title: Web and data security
scopeHtml: Scope: TLS, OWASP top 10 for designers, secrets management, encryption at rest and in transit, key rotation. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Threat modelling first
notes.html:
Security design starts by asking "who would attack this, what do they want, and how would they get in?" Without that you bolt on random controls.

Mechanism: draw the data-flow diagram, mark trust boundaries (internet to edge, edge to services, service to DB, your cloud to a third party), and run STRIDE on each crossing: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Rank by impact times likelihood, then pick controls. Assume breach: any single layer will fail, so layer defences (defence in depth) and give each component least privilege.

Worked example. Payments app: crown jewels are card data and user PII. Threats: stolen DB backup (encrypt at rest, keys in KMS), SQL injection (parameterised queries, least-privilege DB user), insider reading rows (audit log, column encryption), DDoS (CDN, rate limit). Four threats, four controls, owners assigned.

Industry examples. Microsoft invented STRIDE; Stripe keeps card numbers in a small isolated vault so most services never see them (shrinking PCI scope); Google's BeyondCorp assumes the internal network is hostile.

Decision gravity. Threat modelling is cheap early and extremely expensive after launch. Choosing to keep sensitive data out of most services (tokenisation) is a one-way door in your favour.

Everyday analogy. Planning a house's security: doors, windows, a safe for jewellery, a dog, and a neighbour who watches. You do not rely on one lock.

Common interview traps.

  • Listing tools (WAF, TLS) without naming the threat each addresses.
  • Forgetting insiders and third-party dependencies.

notes.title: TLS: encryption in transit
notes.html:
TLS makes a connection private (nobody can read it), authentic (you talk to the real server) and tamper-proof. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.

Mechanism (TLS 1.3, 1 round trip): client sends ClientHello with supported ciphers and a key share (ECDHE); server replies with its key share, its certificate (public key signed by a CA) and a signature proving it holds the private key; both derive session keys; bulk data then uses AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Forward secrecy: session keys are ephemeral, so stealing the server's private key later does not decrypt recorded traffic. TLS 1.3 resumption (0-RTT) saves a round trip but 0-RTT data can be replayed, so use it only for idempotent requests.

# nginx
ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/acme.crt;
ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/acme.key;
add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;
ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:50m;   # about 200k sessions

Worked example. A 100 ms RTT user: TCP handshake 100 ms + TLS 1.2 (2 RTT) 200 ms = 300 ms before the first byte; TLS 1.3 = 200 ms; with session resumption and a CDN edge terminating at 10 ms RTT, it drops to about 30 ms. Crypto CPU on modern hardware (AES-NI) is under 1% of a request, so "TLS is slow" is a myth.

Industry examples. Let's Encrypt issues free 90-day certificates (about 300M sites); Cloudflare and AWS ALB/CloudFront terminate TLS at the edge; Google enforces HTTPS via HSTS preload.

Decision gravity. Terminate at the edge and re-encrypt inside (or use mTLS) is easy to change. Dropping internal encryption "because it is a private network" is a decision attackers exploit after one foothold (NSA/Google SSL-added-and-removed-here incident).

Everyday analogy. Passing sealed, tamper-evident envelopes through a courier, after checking the recipient's ID with a notary (the CA).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying TLS protects data at rest.
  • Forgetting certificate expiry monitoring (outages at Microsoft Teams, Spotify and Equifax were expired certificates).
  • Not mentioning HSTS (stops downgrade to HTTP).

notes.title: mTLS and service-to-service security
notes.html:
Mutual TLS means both sides present certificates, so each service proves who it is. Inside a cluster this replaces "anyone on the network is trusted".

Mechanism: a private CA (or SPIFFE/SPIRE, Istio's Citadel, Linkerd identity) issues each workload a short-lived certificate (for example 24 h) naming its identity spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api. The sidecar proxy or library does the handshake, so app code is unchanged. Authorisation policies then say "only orders may call payments".

# Istio: require mTLS in a namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata: {name: default, namespace: prod}
spec: {mtls: {mode: STRICT}}

Worked example. 500 services, certs rotated every 24 h: 500 renewals/day, trivial for the CA, and a stolen cert is useless after a day. Handshake overhead is amortised by long-lived connections (HTTP/2 or gRPC).

Industry examples. Google ALTS, Lyft/Envoy, Netflix, Istio, Linkerd and AWS App Mesh. Zero-trust architectures (BeyondCorp) use the same idea for users.

Decision gravity. Starting with permissive mode, then moving to strict, is the safe path. Doing it late means a long migration.

Everyday analogy. Both people at the door show ID, not just the visitor.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing mTLS (who is calling) with user authorisation (what the user may do).
  • Long-lived certs that are never rotated.

notes.title: OWASP Top 10 for designers
notes.html:
The OWASP Top 10 lists the most common web flaws; designers should know the design-level cause and the structural fix of each. (2021 list; confirm for newer editions.)

# Risk Design-level fix
A01 Broken access control Deny by default, central authz, object-level checks
A02 Cryptographic failures TLS everywhere, strong algorithms, no secrets in code
A03 Injection (SQL, NoSQL, command, XSS) Parameterised queries, output encoding, CSP
A04 Insecure design Threat model, abuse cases, rate limits
A05 Security misconfiguration Hardened images, IaC scanning, no default creds
A06 Vulnerable components SBOM, dependency scanning, patch SLAs
A07 Identification and auth failures MFA, rate limit, secure sessions
A08 Software and data integrity failures Signed artifacts, CI/CD protection, no unsafe deserialisation
A09 Logging and monitoring failures Audit logs, alerting
A10 SSRF Egress allowlist, block metadata IPs 
// vulnerable
stmt.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + name + "'");
// safe
PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?");
ps.setString(1, name);

Worked example. SSRF: an image-URL fetcher lets an attacker request http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/, which returns cloud credentials. Fix: block link-local and private ranges, use IMDSv2 (token required), egress through a proxy with an allowlist, and give the instance a minimal IAM role.

Industry examples. Capital One 2019 breach combined SSRF, a misconfigured WAF and an over-privileged role (100M records). Log4Shell (2021, A06) hit almost every Java shop. Equifax 2017 was an unpatched Struts library.

Decision gravity. Parameterised queries and framework output encoding are free and should be non-negotiable. Retrofitting access-control checks across 200 endpoints is expensive; do it via middleware from the start.

Everyday analogy. A pre-flight checklist: every item exists because a plane once crashed for lack of it.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting the list without a fix for each.
  • Thinking a WAF replaces secure code (it is a speed bump, not a wall).
  • Forgetting XSS and CSRF defences for cookie-based apps (CSP, SameSite, CSRF tokens).

notes.title: Secrets management
notes.html:
A secret is any credential (DB password, API key, signing key). Keep it out of code, images and logs, and fetch it at runtime from a dedicated store.

Mechanism: a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, K8s secrets backed by KMS or External Secrets Operator) stores values encrypted, enforces IAM per secret, logs every access, and supports versions and rotation. Apps authenticate with their workload identity (IAM role, K8s service account), not with another static secret (avoids the "secret zero" problem). Prefer dynamic secrets: Vault creates a DB user valid for 1 h per request and drops it.

# Vault dynamic Postgres creds (lease 1h)
vault read database/creds/orders-ro
# username v-orders-ro-8fj2  password A1a-...  lease_duration 1h
# CI hygiene
gitleaks detect --source . ; git log -p | grep -i 'AKIA'

Worked example. 300 services x average 3 secrets = 900 secrets. Static secrets rotated quarterly = 3,600 rotations/year, impossible by hand, so automate. Dynamic secrets: leak window shrinks from months to 1 hour.

Industry examples. Uber (2016) lost AWS keys committed to a private GitHub repo (57M accounts); Toyota and others leaked keys in public repos for years. Netflix, Airbnb and Stripe use Vault-style systems with per-service identity.

Decision gravity. Introducing a secrets manager is cheap early. Rotating a secret baked into 40 deployed apps is a one-way, painful migration. Plan for rotation (apps must reload or support two valid versions).

Everyday analogy. A hotel safe with a log: staff get the combination for one shift only, instead of writing it on the wall.

Common interview traps.

  • Env vars in the image or docker inspect / crash dumps exposing them; mounted files or runtime fetch are better.
  • Committing .env files; deleting the commit does not remove the leak (rotate it).
  • Same secret across dev and prod.

notes.title: Encryption at rest
notes.html:
Encryption at rest protects stored data if disks, snapshots or backups are stolen. It does not stop a logged-in attacker or a SQL injection, because the DB decrypts for them.

Layers, from broad to fine:

  1. Full-disk / volume (EBS, LUKS, BitLocker): transparent, near-zero cost (AES-NI), covers lost disks.
  2. Database TDE (Postgres via disk or extensions, SQL Server/Oracle TDE, RDS storage encryption).
  3. Application-level / field-level: the app encrypts specific columns (card number, SSN) before writing; the DB and its admins see ciphertext only.

Envelope encryption is the pattern: a data key (DEK) encrypts the data (AES-256-GCM); a key encryption key (KEK) in KMS/HSM encrypts the DEK; you store the encrypted DEK next to the data. KMS is called only to unwrap DEKs, so you can re-key by re-wrapping tiny DEKs rather than re-encrypting terabytes.

# envelope sketch (AWS)
dk = kms.generate_data_key(KeyId="alias/orders", KeySpec="AES_256")
ct = AESGCM(dk["Plaintext"]).encrypt(nonce, plaintext, aad)   # unique nonce every time
store(ct, nonce, dk["CiphertextBlob"])   # wrapped DEK stored with the data

Worked example. 10 TB of S3 objects with one DEK per object: re-keying the KEK touches 10M small wrapped DEKs (minutes), not 10 TB of data (days). KMS costs about $0.03 per 10,000 requests, so cache DEKs in memory for a few minutes at 5k requests/s.

Industry examples. S3 SSE-KMS, RDS and EBS encryption, Google Tink library, Stripe encrypting card data with per-record keys in an HSM-backed vault, MongoDB Client-Side Field Level Encryption.

Decision gravity. Disk-level is a free default (turn it on at creation; enabling later may require a copy). Field-level encryption is a heavy one-way door: you lose indexing and search on those columns (use deterministic encryption or blind indexes, with trade-offs).

Everyday analogy. Locking your valuables in a box and putting the box key in the bank vault; to change the lock you swap the box key, not move all the valuables.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "encrypted at rest" protects against app-level breaches.
  • Reusing a GCM nonce (breaks security catastrophically).
  • Storing the key next to the data.

notes.title: Encryption in transit vs at rest
notes.html:
In transit protects data moving between machines (TLS, mTLS, VPN, SSH); at rest protects stored bytes; "in use" (memory) is covered by enclaves. You need both because each covers a different attacker.

Hop Control
Browser to edge TLS 1.3, HSTS
Edge to service TLS re-encrypt or mTLS
Service to DB TLS (sslmode=verify-full in Postgres)
Service to Kafka TLS + SASL/mTLS listeners
Disk, backups, snapshots Volume or object encryption with KMS
Hot fields Field-level encryption
End-to-end Client-held keys (Signal, WhatsApp)

End-to-end encryption (E2EE): only the endpoints hold keys, the server sees ciphertext. WhatsApp and Signal use the Signal protocol (X3DH key agreement + Double Ratchet, giving forward secrecy per message). Trade-off: the server cannot search, moderate, or restore history without client-side help; multi-device and group chats need key distribution design.

Worked example. A Kafka cluster with TLS on every listener: CPU overhead is typically 10 to 30%, and zero-copy sendfile is lost for consumer fetches. Plan capacity with this in mind (confirm for your version and hardware).

Industry examples. Postgres sslmode=verify-full, Redis 6+ TLS, Kafka SSL listeners, Cloudflare Keyless SSL (private key stays in the customer's HSM).

Decision gravity. TLS everywhere is reversible config; E2EE is a one-way product decision because it prevents server-side features forever.

Everyday analogy. Armoured van for the road (in transit), vault in the bank (at rest), and a sealed letter only the recipient can open (E2EE).

Common interview traps.

  • Using sslmode=require (no certificate verification) and thinking it is safe from man-in-the-middle.
  • Forgetting backups, logs and analytics copies; they carry the same data.

notes.title: Key management and rotation
notes.html:
Keys must be generated, stored, used, rotated and destroyed with controls; the key is the real secret, not the algorithm.

Mechanism: keep root keys in an HSM or cloud KMS (keys never leave, you send data to be encrypted or wrapped). Separate keys by purpose and tenant (signing vs encryption; one KEK per environment or customer). Rotation limits the amount of data under one key and the damage of a leak:

  • KEK rotation (cheap): new KMS key version; new wraps use it; old versions remain for decrypt (AWS can auto-rotate yearly; re-wrap lazily).
  • DEK rotation: re-encrypt data in the background, or use per-object keys that age out.
  • Signing key rotation (JWT/JWKS): publish both old and new public keys by kid, start signing with the new, keep old for at least one token lifetime, then remove.
  • Compromise rotation is urgent: revoke, re-issue, re-encrypt, then investigate.
day 0   JWKS: [k1]        sign with k1
day 30  JWKS: [k1, k2]    sign with k2  (gateways pick up k2 via cache TTL 1h)
day 31  JWKS: [k2]        k1 tokens (15 min TTL) all expired

Worked example. AES-GCM with random 96-bit nonces is safe for about 2^32 (4 billion) messages per key; at 10k encryptions/s a key lasts about 5 days before you should rotate, which is why per-object DEKs or key-per-day schemes are used.

Industry examples. AWS KMS (FIPS 140-2 HSMs, automatic rotation), Google Cloud KMS, HashiCorp Vault transit engine ("encryption as a service"), Let's Encrypt automating 90-day cert rotation, Microsoft's 2023 Storm-0558 incident (a stolen signing key minted tokens).

Decision gravity. Design rotation in from day one: encrypted blobs should store a key version id. Without that, rotation becomes a risky one-way migration.

Everyday analogy. Changing the locks on a building on a schedule, and keeping a ring of old keys for rooms you have not yet re-keyed.

Common interview traps.

  • Rotating a key by deleting the old one (data becomes unreadable).
  • No overlap window, so valid tokens suddenly fail verification.
  • Same key for signing and encryption.

notes.title: Web hardening checklist
notes.html:
A few headers and habits close many holes cheaply.

  • CORS: allow only specific origins; never * with credentials.
  • CSP: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self' limits XSS impact.
  • Cookies: HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax.
  • Input: validate on the server (type, length, allowlist), encode on output, parameterise queries.
  • File uploads: random names, size cap, content-type sniffing, store outside web root (S3 with private ACL and pre-signed URLs), virus scan.
  • Dependencies: Dependabot/Renovate, npm audit, SBOM, pinned base images.
  • Least privilege: DB user for the app has no DROP; IAM roles scoped per service.
  • Errors: no stack traces to clients; log full detail internally.
  • Logging: never log passwords, tokens, card numbers or full PII; add request IDs.
add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;
add_header X-Frame-Options DENY always;
add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'" always;
add_header Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin always;

Worked example. Upload of a 2 GB video: instead of proxying through your app (ties up a worker for minutes), issue a pre-signed S3 PUT URL valid 10 min, with a size and content-type condition; client uploads direct to S3; an event triggers scanning and processing.

Industry examples. Slack, GitHub and Google ship strict CSP; Mozilla Observatory grades sites on these headers; pre-signed URLs are used by Dropbox-style and Instagram-style upload paths.

Decision gravity. All reversible config, cheap, and high value; skipping them is the common failure, not misjudging them.

Everyday analogy. Locking the windows and not leaving a spare key under the mat: boring, effective.

Common interview traps.

  • CORS treated as a security boundary for servers (it only controls browsers).
  • Logging full request bodies "for debugging".

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Threat model first (STRIDE, trust boundaries); layer defences and use least privilege.
  • TLS 1.3 gives privacy, authenticity, integrity and forward secrecy; terminate at the edge but re-encrypt inside, and use mTLS between services with short-lived certs.
  • Know OWASP Top 10 with a design fix each: deny-by-default authz, parameterised queries, patched dependencies, SSRF egress controls, audit logging.
  • Secrets live in a secrets manager with workload identity; prefer dynamic short-lived secrets; leaked secrets must be rotated, not just deleted.
  • Encryption at rest uses envelope encryption (DEK wrapped by a KMS KEK); disk-level is a free default, field-level is a heavy trade-off; protects stolen media, not app breaches.
  • Rotate keys by versioning (store key id with the blob), overlap old and new, and never delete a key that still has data under it.
  • Harden basics: HSTS, CSP, cookie flags, strict CORS, safe uploads with pre-signed URLs, no secrets or PII in logs.
